article.title: Why Customer Migration Tables Need Both Rates and Absolute Numbers
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A migration table shows how customers move between tiers, deciles, or behavioral states over time. Percentages make patterns easy to compare, but percentages alone can create a misleading picture of business impact. Imagine that 40 percent of a small group of 1,000 customers upgrades, while only 5 percent of a group of 200,000 upgrades. The first group has a much higher rate, but the second produces far more upgraded customers in absolute terms. Both views are necessary. Rates describe the probability or intensity of movement within a starting population. Counts describe operational scale and potential economic impact. A good transition matrix therefore includes the starting base, destination counts, and row percentages. It can also show revenue or margin associated with each movement. Denominators must be explicit. An upgrade rate based on customers who were eligible at the start is different from a rate based only on customers observed in both years. Excluding churned customers can make retention and migration look artificially strong. Entry and exit should be represented rather than silently removed. Cohort size can also change over time. A tier may grow because many new customers enter it, not because existing customers upgrade. Separating retained customers, new entrants, upgrades, downgrades, and exits prevents this composition effect from being mistaken for behavioral improvement. Statistical uncertainty matters for small groups. A 30 percent rate based on ten customers is much less stable than a 30 percent rate based on ten thousand. Confidence intervals or minimum-base rules can prevent overreaction to noisy cells. Business interpretation should connect movement to value. Moving 5,000 customers from Silver to Gold is attractive only if their incremental contribution exceeds the cost of Gold benefits and any incentives used to move them. Analysts should also examine distance moved. A one-level upgrade and a three-level upgrade may have different mechanisms and economic meanings. Sankey diagrams can help communication, but the underlying table should remain auditable. The main lesson is simple: rates answer how common a movement is; counts answer how large it is. Management needs both to understand whether a migration pattern is strategically important.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
